prompt: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together, because both go up in hot weather.
tells: because both go up in hot weather
why: Hot weather sells ice cream and sends people swimming, so both rise together. A third factor driving two things is a confounder.
trap: The link is real; the cause is a third thing.

prompt: Kids with bigger shoes read better, since older kids have both.
why: Older kids have bigger feet and read better, so shoe size and reading move together. Age is the confounder behind both.

prompt: Coffee drinkers seemed to have more heart disease, until smoking was taken into account.
tells: until smoking was taken into account
why: Coffee drinkers smoked more, and smoking causes heart disease. Once smoking was accounted for, the coffee link faded. Smoking was the confounder.
trap: The data wasn't unrepresentative; a factor was missing.

prompt: Hospitals with more doctors have more deaths, because they treat sicker patients.
why: Big hospitals with more doctors take the sickest patients, who die more often. How ill the patients are is the confounder, not the doctors.

prompt: Fires with more firefighters show more damage, because bigger fires bring both.
why: Big fires bring more firefighters and cause more damage. Fire size drives both, so it's a confounder, not the firefighters.

prompt: A study compares people of the same age and income so that a hidden third factor doesn't fool it.
why: Comparing people with the same age and income removes those as explanations for any difference. That's controlling for confounders.
trap: It's not about who was sampled.
